title: Twinkle Khanna and Dimple Kapadia Are Making Paneer at Home. The Fake Paneer Crisis Made Them Do It.
excerpt: The author and her mother have turned to homemade paneer amid India's growing food adulteration scandal, sparking a family rivalry over whose kitchen produces more.
body:
• Author Twinkle Khanna has revealed that she and her mother, veteran actor Dimple Kapadia, have started making paneer at home in response to India's fake paneer crisis.
  • Their paneer-making has become a source of family rivalry, with Dimple claiming a higher yield of 250 grams per litre of milk compared to Twinkle's 180 grams.
  • Maharashtra recently imposed a one-year ban on analogue paneer after 35% of tested samples failed quality standards, and FSSAI is pushing for a nationwide crackdown.
  • The homemade paneer trend reflects growing consumer distrust of commercially sold paneer in India, driven by widespread adulteration scandals.

Twinkle Khanna, the bestselling author and former actor, has joined a growing number of Indians turning to homemade paneer after the fake paneer crisis made national headlines. In her latest Times of India column, Khanna revealed that she and her mother, veteran Bollywood actor Dimple Kapadia, have both taken to making paneer at home — though not without some competitive friction.

A Mother-Daughter Paneer Rivalry

The household dairy operation has sparked a characteristically humorous family dispute. According to Khanna, Dimple Kapadia insists that her kitchen produces 250 grams of paneer from a single litre of milk, while Twinkle's household manages just 180 grams from the same quantity.

For Dimple, the gap was not simply about technique — it was, as Twinkle relayed with her signature deadpan humor, evidence of "maternal failure." The anecdote captures a broader cultural moment: India's paneer crisis has pushed families to take dairy matters into their own hands.

What Is Driving the Fake Paneer Panic?

The Khanna household's shift to homemade paneer comes amid an escalating food safety crisis. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration imposed a sweeping one-year ban on analogue paneer in August 2026, after testing revealed alarming levels of adulteration. Of 308 paneer and dairy analogue samples tested between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 — over 35% — failed quality standards. Thirty samples were declared unsafe for consumption.

Laboratory investigations found that natural milk fat had been replaced with cheap vegetable oils, palm oil, starches, and other non-dairy ingredients in many products. While analogue paneer mimics the appearance and texture of traditional paneer, it lacks essential nutrients — a serious concern for India's millions of vegetarians who rely on paneer as a primary protein source.

A Nationwide Crackdown

Maharashtra's ban is part of a broader regulatory push. The FSSAI has ordered a nationwide enforcement drive, directing all states to intensify inspections across the dairy supply chain. Gujarat mandated that eateries declare whether they use real or analogue paneer. The Consumer Affairs Ministry is considering requiring restaurants to disclose paneer substitutes on menus.

Celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor recently weighed in on the debate, clarifying that analogue paneer is not inherently "fake" — it is approved under FSSAI regulations — but stressed that consumers must be clearly informed about what they are buying. The distinction between mislabeled substitutes and genuinely adulterated products has become a key part of the public conversation.

For the Diaspora, Homemade Is the Norm

For Indian families abroad, making paneer at home has always been standard practice — fresh paneer is rarely available at mainstream supermarkets, and imported options often lack the texture and taste of the real thing. The process is straightforward: boil full-cream milk, curdle it with lemon juice or vinegar, strain through muslin cloth, and press under a weight.

What is new is that families in India are now adopting the same habit — driven not by scarcity, but by distrust. When even a bestselling author with means and access prefers to make paneer at home, it speaks to how deeply the adulteration crisis has shaken consumer confidence.
